newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TRANSPORT - NRC sees no threat from private sector.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AUSTRALIA TRANSPORT - NRC sees no threat from private sector.

text.p: Public rail freight firm National Rail Corp (NRC) does not view the consortium formed by private rail operators TNT Ltd and Toll Holdings Ltd as a competitive threat, NRC chief Vince Graham said.

"In no way shape or form do I see the Toll/TNT announcement as a competitive threat. I think it is a demonstration of the confidence that the private sector now has to be involved in the rail industry," Graham said in an interview with Reuters.
TNT and Toll announced on Monday they had signed a heads of agreement to form a consortium to operate rail freight services.
Earlier this year, Toll signed an agreement for NRC to undertake Toll's linehaul service on the national network.
"I'm seeing at the moment TNT and Toll as a potential purchaser of National Rail," Graham said.

Under the shareholder agreement that established NRC in 1993, the company's three shareholders, the Federal Government and the state governments of Victoria and New South Wales have the opportunity to sell their shareholdings from February 1998.

Graham said National Rail's prize assets were the 120 high-tech locomotives the company had ordered over the next year, as well as its large investment in low tier container wagons and capital city terminal upgrades.
"Most importantly, (there is) the investment we have made in information technology to support the business and to support the logistics business," he said.
Graham said NRC was keen to reduce costs.
NRC had clear cost-cutting targets in place and believed it could win improvements in its asset utilisation productivity.
"On the east coast Melbourne-Sydney-Brisbane corridor, unless you have a cost structure that competes with a B-double truck, you may as well not be in the business," Graham said.
Graham said the rail industry controlled about 55 to 60 percent of the freight carried on the east west corridor, sourced in Sydney-Melbourne-Adelaide-Perth and vice versa.
On the east coast, Adelaide-Melbourne-Sydney-Brisbane corridor, the rail industry had only 30 percent of the market and just 20 percent of the Melbourne-Sydney market, Graham said.
"There is room in both of the corridors for rail to lift market share, the first is getting service quality that is more reliable and more acceptable to the market place,"
NRC's new locomotives were a substantial improvement that would make an big difference to the reliability of rail services, Graham said.
Graham said the new locomtives had a variable horsepower feature which was important for economising on fuel.

"The tonnage moving to the west is three times the tonnage moving to the east. You are obviously bringing back lighter trains than you are sending over. Being able to effectively vary your horsepower on the back haul is an important advantage."

NRC has committed more than A$1 billion on the development and ongoing maintenance of the new fleet of locomotives which are rolling off the production line at the Newcastle plant of A. Goninan & Co. Ltd, a subsidiary of Howard Smith Ltd.
